title: Agentic AI Chat
description: Leveraging AI experiences to create valuable outcomes for customers.
blurb: Embedded with product engineers, I led end-to-end UX for a conversational AI agent now used across observability tools by 10,000+ LinkedIn engineers. I set the UX principles for LLM-powered interactions, spec'd the contextual input, plugins, and inline-artifact components the team builds on, and designed a custom icon system that signals a trusted, purpose-built tool. The result is faster incident triage and lower cognitive load for engineers working mid-incident.

hero.alt: Observe Agent chat home screen, embedded in the observability product

sections.heading: Overview
body: As **Product Designer** at LinkedIn, I collaborated closely with product engineers to design a front-end conversational experience for an AI agent for observability products used by 10,000 employees. The result was a major decrease in the time it takes developers to find root causes for performance incidents such as service disruptions and network latency.
**Outcome:** faster incident triage, lower cognitive load, a trusted AI surface.

sections.heading: AI in Context

image.alt: The agent conversation shown alongside a logs explorer view, sharing context with the surrounding UI

body: One product design goal was to create a **conversational assistant** that feels native to LinkedIn engineers, and seamlessly integrated with existing views so that user and agent can chat in context with adjacent UI elements.

sections.heading: UI Principles

image.alt: Storyboard of side-panel placement options, showing how the chat panel shares screen space with the existing application

body: To help the team decide how the chat experience shares screen real estate with the existing application, and to establish meaningful placement of side panels, I conducted an audit of existing panels and used a basic storyboard to communicate the **design rationale** for panel placement.

sections.heading: Elements and Interactions

image.alt: Interaction specs for chat input, plugins menu, contextual tags, and inline chart artifacts

body: To help developers move fast, I spec'd critical elements and interactions with a thoughtful **design language**. Critical components include plugins, contextual input, and inline artifacts such as charts. These components enable better contextual input and quicker answers for the user.

sections.heading: User Needs

image.alt: User-needs statements from a Site Reliability Engineer persona, framed as "I want to…" jobs

body: The primary persona is a Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) or an on-call engineer in mid-incident. Before designing anything, I outlined some basic user needs to align the team on what we were building.
**Common context:** high-pressure, multi-tab workflows, fragmented tooling across alerts, metrics, logs, and deployments.

sections.heading: Branding

image.alt: Icon design work: a comparison audit of sparkle glyphs and the final telescope-plus-sparkle mark in its variations

body: I created custom graphical icons instead of using a generic bot icon. A custom icon reinforces the custom solution as a trusted tool.

Icon design work started with a comparison audit to uncover best practices and recognizable patterns. The final design used sparkle glyphs to indicate AI and the shape of a telescope to indicate Observe. I created variations for multiple experience channels such as the application UI and Slack.

title: Genomic Data Platform
description: Tools for scientists to analyze genomic data for pharmaceutical and clinical needs.
blurb: As Senior Staff Interaction Designer, I led UX across Illumina's Connected Analytics platform for multiomic analysis, spanning genomics, proteomics, and spatial transcriptomics apps built on a shared design system, data model, and user base. I grounded the work in evidence-based personas, card sorting with bioinformaticians, and ongoing field research, then turned direct customer feedback into shipped visualization features. The result is a cohesive platform that helps scientists compare groups of subjects and accelerate biomarker and drug discovery.
team: UX researchers, bioinformatics subject-matter experts, product stakeholders

hero.alt: The Cohorts survival-comparison view: a Kaplan–Meier curve comparing subject groups with a p-value matrix

blocks.value: Cohorts, by Illumina Connected Analytics, lets customers aggregate and analyze genomic and clinical data using private, public and partner data sets, and then compare groups of subjects to **accelerate biomarker and drug discovery**.

As **Senior Staff Interaction Designer** at Illumina, I created personas based on interviews with stakeholders and subject matter experts. These **evidence-based personas** were used to identify user behaviors, tasks, and workflows. The key persona is the research scientist whose goal is to discover biomarkers of interest for pharmaceutical or clinical cures.

blocks.alt: Personas for the genomics scientist, bioinformatician, and developer/admin, with goals and a pain-point quote

blocks.value: The discovery phase is one of my favorite parts of the design process. I collaborated with UX researchers and conducted a series of card sorting activities with subject matter experts and stakeholders to better understand the terminology and **mental models** for analyzing genomic data.

blocks.alt: A remote card sorting session grouping genomic analysis terms into workflow phases

blocks.value: Early low-fidelity conceptual designs helped identify **interaction models**, and user interviews helped validate the concepts. I conducted several user interviews with bioinformaticians currently using digital workflows to evaluate genetic variants.

blocks.alt: Low-fidelity cohort-builder prototypes shown to bioinformaticians in interview sessions

blocks.value: Storyboards help communicate to product stakeholders the high-level design of the **user workflows** and **interaction models**.

blocks.alt: A storyboard grid walking through building a cohort, visualizing distributions, and comparing survival outcomes

blocks.value: Prototypes are invaluable UX tools for communicating the **experience design** decisions to stakeholders and users. In this screenshot from Figma, the blue arrows, nicknamed “noodles,” are the interactive connections within the prototype.

blocks.alt: A Figma prototype canvas with many screens connected by blue interaction arrows

blocks.value: This end-to-end design journey included several **user research studies** and ongoing synthesis of **customer feedback** from scientific users in the field.

blocks.alt: A recorded customer call with a researcher describing the need for a gene-discovery heat map

blocks.value: In this example, I used direct customer feedback to uncover an **unmet user need** to discover genes that are relevant to their scientific studies. My resulting mockups specified new user-centered features such as a comparison heat map.

blocks.alt: A gene comparison heat map showing variant frequency and type across genes for two cohorts

blocks.value: I use insights from **user testing** to identify incremental product improvements. For example, allowing users to customize a data visualization plot based on their research needs.

blocks.alt: A user-testing session where a participant asks to invert the y-axis so rare variants are visible

blocks.value: User testing also uncovered unmet user needs to view the distribution of variants by type, and since there were several types to measure per gene, the radar charts were an appropriate and intuitive **data visualization**.

blocks.alt: A grid of radar charts showing structural-variant type distribution per gene

blocks.value: I applied the visual design language and interaction patterns to related apps to ensure that the platform of products have a **cohesive look and feel**.

blocks.alt: The Connected Multiomics proteomics viewer with a volcano plot and per-protein box plots
The Connected Multiomics spatial viewer showing a tissue slice with a UMAP and transcript counts

title: AI Recommendations
description: Using machine learning to create valuable outcomes for customers.
blurb: As Principal UX Designer, I brought AI-predicted best practices into Informatica's data-integration products, designing an inline recommendation model that suggests the next set of transformations without breaking the developer's flow. I partnered with ML engineers to shape the interaction model across cloud and desktop, and designed a lightweight precision-tracking method that I convinced cross-functional teams to ship, so the model retrains on real user choices.
team: Machine learning engineers, UX researchers, UX partners, executive leadership

hero.alt: The data-integration mapping canvas with an AI recommendations panel suggesting next transformations

blocks.value: As **Principal User Experience Designer** at Informatica, I designed a new product feature using artificial intelligence to predict and recommend best practices in data workflows.

The **AI model** is trained on anonymized mappings across multiple customer tenants. A mapping is a data transformation workflow that moves data from a source to a target with user-specified transformations in between. I collaborated with machine learning engineers and UX researchers to identify user behaviors and determine the most appropriate **interaction model** and user experience for both cloud and desktop products.

blocks.alt: The mapping designer shown in both the desktop client and the cloud product

blocks.value: The machine learning model determines best practices by analyzing matching sequences within transformations, and based on prior usage patterns produces recommendations for the “next set” of transforms to add during development.

blocks.alt: The transformation menu with AI-recommended options marked by a distinct icon

blocks.value: I advocated to integrate the **AI recommendations** so that the experience was seamless within existing user workflows, and the best example I found to tell this story was predictive text in text apps.

blocks.alt: A messaging app suggesting the next words inline, used as an analogy for inline transformation recommendations

blocks.value: Predictive text is seamlessly integrated with the existing user workflow and not disruptive or jarring.
Early conceptual sketches and renderings helped identify conceptual models for the inline recommendations.

blocks.alt: Hand sketches exploring where and how recommendations could appear in the mapping canvas
Higher-fidelity renderings of the recommendation menu and inline affordances

blocks.value: In addition to creating **interactive prototypes**, I use animation to help define interaction paradigms — it's an effective way to communicate concepts to stakeholders and developers.

blocks.alt: An animated prototype showing a recommendation appearing and being accepted in the mapping canvas

blocks.value: Early storyboards helped identify interaction models for a panel concept.

blocks.alt: A storyboard walking through when recommendations surface, how they are explained, and how they are accepted or dismissed
Visual explorations applying Informatica's CLAIRE AI branding to the recommendations panel

blocks.value: My **user-centered design** approach identified the primary persona as the Data Integration Developer. The **business objectives** introduced another target persona identified by the technology research and consulting firm Gartner: the Citizen Integrator, a non-technical subject-matter expert who needs data integration tools without code.

blocks.alt: The two target personas: the Data Integration Developer and the non-technical Citizen Integrator

blocks.value: While conducting user research, I observed customers using the newly released features. **Users think the end results are pretty cool.**

blocks.alt: A customer quote: “Since the last upgrade they added this function that's pretty cool.”

blocks.value: To ensure the **accuracy of the model**, I designed a simple method to measure user choices against the generated predictions and convinced cross-functional teams to implement the tracking. When there are false positives, the model updates to reflect the most common user decisions.

blocks.alt: A diagram contrasting a true-positive and a false-positive prediction, feeding user selections back to improve the model

blocks.value: I worked closely with UX partners to redesign the product look and feel, then convinced executive leadership that modernizing the UI was a sound business goal.

blocks.alt: Before-and-after of the mapping designer showing the modernized visual design language

title: Developer Experience
description: Guiding software developers through a cloud-based data platform experience.
outcome: Senior Staff UX Designer + acting TPM · Led MVP to launch
role: Senior Staff UX Interaction Designer and acting Technical Product Manager, GE Digital

sections.heading: Overview
body: I led design — and for a stretch, product management — for a new web portal and administration console for a cloud platform's services, built from scratch with an agile team.

sections.heading: The problem
body: Developers needed a way to find, understand, and adopt cloud services that didn't exist yet. The design centered on a primary user, "Elaine the Software Architect," and the decisions she makes along her journey.

sections.heading: Approach
body: A persona-driven strategy tied every feature to a point in Elaine's path.
items: Product storyboards to identify the critical features along the journey
Wireframes and After Effects motion prototypes to test interaction paradigms
An adoption strategy aimed at developers, built on instructional web videos
Directing a lean video crew to produce hands-on coding-tip content

sections.heading: Outcomes
body: We shipped an MVP catalog of cloud services quickly, demoed it to analysts including Gartner, and launched the full product months later. I then moved into a product manager role, presenting at GE's Minds + Machines and Industrial Internet events.

title: Machine Learning for Operators
description: Enabling operations engineers to train AI models for accuracy.
role: Senior Staff UX Interaction Designer, GE Digital
team: Product managers and international scrum teams across California, Bangalore, and New York; UX researchers

sections.heading: Overview
body: Training an accurate AI model normally takes a data scientist. The operations engineers closest to industrial sensor data don't have that background. This work aimed to get machine-learning techniques into the hands of industrialists by reducing the complexity of the process.

sections.heading: The problem
body: The people with the deepest understanding of the equipment and its data were locked out of model training by tooling that assumed data-science expertise.

sections.heading: Approach
body: Design followed the iterative shape of the data-science process itself.
items: Product strategy with stakeholders and scrum teams across three regions to align roadmaps and keep the experience consistent
Contextual observation of reliability engineers, data analysts, and data scientists on customer sites
Data curation and exploration tools so users could evaluate data before and after training
Prognostic equipment dashboards designed for low-light industrial environments
Monitoring tools to detect data drift and flag when a model needs retraining

title: Operational Insights
description: Solutions to help development teams monitor and analyze operational data.
outcome: Principal UX Designer · Shipped; positive customer feedback
team: One UX designer (Jim Reed) and one UX researcher

sections.heading: Overview
body: Small teams — typically five or fewer developers and one manager — both build data jobs and monitor the daily flow of data through them. I designed a monitoring experience shaped around how those teams actually check in on their work.

sections.heading: The problem
body: The "Monday-morning check" of data-integration jobs is a glance, not an analysis session. Traditional dashboard visualizations like pie charts didn't match what people needed in that first look.

sections.heading: Approach
body: Interviews and workflow observations produced a two-tier model for the dashboard.
items: Big numbers, first glance — large, actionable "fast facts" (Rows Processed, Number of Jobs) with stacked column charts for job-status breakdowns
Analysis views, second glance — detailed visualizations, including line charts to correlate metrics with projects or folders over time
A proposed Slack app for collaborative operations monitoring, inspired by teams' pieced-together workflows
Color coding for AI predictions — blue for actual values, green for predicted
Dropping an early logo-based mockup that wouldn't scale to hundreds of connector types

sections.heading: Outcomes
body: Post-launch feedback confirmed the design met customers' needs, with users specifically calling out that it showed "the right kinds of metrics."
[Outcome metric placeholder]

title: Mobile Emergency System
description: A next-generation 911 service enables collaboration between emergency dispatchers and responders.

sections.heading: Overview
body: A next-generation 911 service that lets emergency dispatchers, operators, responders, and citizens share critical information during an incident. I designed the system across iOS, Android, and desktop.

sections.heading: The problem
body: Emergencies demand fast, multi-directional communication between people in very different roles and contexts. The design goal was to make a genuinely complex system feel simple to use under stress.

sections.heading: Approach
body: Storyboard sketches formed the base for the UX flows, followed by wireframes and high-fidelity mockups.
items: Motion studies to animate the UI for different emergency scenarios and keep transitions seamless
Mood boards to set the aesthetic direction for emergency alerting
Emergency situation tracking — citizens check in with location data and receive operator alerts
Interactive maps — operators publish layers and pins so responders and civilians can track incidents and cordons

title: Additive Manufacturing
description: Enabling people at work, optimizing innovative technologies and processes.
role: Senior Staff UX Interaction Designer, GE Digital

sections.heading: Overview
body: Customers running industrial 3D laser printers needed visibility into how their machines were operating. I designed a dashboard that gathers sensor data and surfaces statistical calculations per printer and across a facility.

sections.heading: The problem
body: An early design showed the Availability Score as a donut chart. User testing found it confusing — the printers themselves already use a similar visualization to show print progress, so the metric read as something it wasn't.

sections.heading: Approach
body: Contextual research at a facility producing aircraft-engine parts grounded the work — observing the manufacturing process and interviewing operators in place.
items: A journey map of roles, tasks, and key personas to identify product opportunities
Replacing the donut chart with a simple number and color indicator after concept testing
Mobile concepts, since operators work on call and need remote status monitoring

sections.heading: Outcomes
body: The shipped dashboard shows an Availability Score for each printer's productivity plus aggregate facility-level metrics.
[Outcome metric placeholder]

title: Analytics & Big Data
description: Enterprise SaaS and platform applications for big data and analytics.
role: Senior Staff UX Interaction Designer, GE Digital
team: Subject-matter experts and stakeholders in collaborative design sessions

sections.heading: Overview
body: Research with data scientists and data engineers kept pointing at the same thing: data exploration and cleansing is a critical part of the data-science process. I conceived Data Explorer to give teams visualization tools for evaluating data before and after analytic processing.

sections.heading: The problem
body: Teams had no good way to see their data — its shape, its quality — at the points in the workflow where that visibility matters most.

sections.heading: Approach
body: I ran collaborative design sessions with subject-matter experts, sketching and mapping task flows with diagrams and sticky notes. Running UX workshops and involving stakeholders directly is a good way to give everyone ownership of the design.
Alongside Data Explorer, a searchable, sortable catalog of data and analytic techniques lets users sequence techniques and business logic together in a tool called the Orchestration Editor.
items: Sketches
Storyboards
User task flows
